CHAPTER XXXVI. MOTHER AND DAUGHTER

Lona was so disgusted with the people, and especially with the women,
that she wished to abandon the place as soon as possible; I, on the
contrary, felt very strongly that to do so would be to fail wilfully
where success was possible; and, far worse, to weaken the hearts of
the Little Ones, and so bring them into much greater danger. If we
retreated, it was certain the princess would not leave us unassailed!
if we encountered her, the hope of the prophecy went with us! Mother
and daughter must meet: it might be that Lona’s loveliness would take
Lilith’s heart by storm! if she threatened violence, I should be there
between them! If I found that I had no other power over her, I was
ready, for the sake of my Lona, to strike her pitilessly on the closed
hand! I knew she was doomed: most likely it was decreed that her doom
should now be brought to pass through us!

Still without hint of the relation in which she stood to the princess,
I stated the case to Lona as it appeared to me. At once she agreed to
accompany me to the palace.

From the top of one of its great towers, the princess had, in the early
morning, while the city yet slept, descried the approach of the army of
the Little Ones. The sight awoke in her an over-mastering terror: she
had failed in her endeavour to destroy them, and they were upon her! The
prophecy was about to be fulfilled!

When she came to herself, she descended to the black hall, and seated
herself in the north focus of the ellipse, under the opening in the
roof.

For she must think! Now what she called THINKING required a clear
consciousness of herself, not as she was, but as she chose to believe
herself; and to aid her in the realisation of this consciousness, she
had suspended, a little way from and above her, itself invisible in the
darkness of the hall, a mirror to receive the full sunlight reflected
from her person. For the resulting vision of herself in the splendour of
her beauty, she sat waiting the meridional sun.

Many a shadow moved about her in the darkness, but as often as, with a
certain inner eye which she had, she caught sight of one, she refused
to regard it. Close under the mirror stood the Shadow which attended her
walks, but, self-occupied, him she did not see.

The city was taken; the inhabitants were cowering in terror; the Little
Ones and their strange cavalry were encamped in the square; the sun
shone upon the princess, and for a few minutes she saw herself glorious.
The vision passed, but she sat on. The night was now come, and darkness
clothed and filled the glass, yet she did not move. A gloom that swarmed
with shadows, wallowed in the palace; the servants shivered and shook,
but dared not leave it because of the beasts of the Little Ones; all
night long the princess sat motionless: she must see her beauty again!
she must try again to think! But courage and will had grown weary of
her, and would dwell with her no more!

In the morning we chose twelve of the tallest and bravest of the boys
to go with us to the palace. We rode our great horses, and they small
horses and elephants.

The princess sat waiting the sun to give her the joy of her own
presence. The tide of the light was creeping up the shore of the sky,
but until the sun stood overhead, not a ray could enter the black hall.

He rose to our eyes, and swiftly ascended. As we climbed the steep way
to the palace, he climbed the dome of its great hall. He looked in at
the eye of it--and with sudden radiance the princess flashed upon her
own sight. But she sprang to her feet with a cry of despair: alas her
whiteness! the spot covered half her side, and was black as the marble
around her! She clutched her robe, and fell back in her chair. The
Shadow glided out, and she saw him go.

We found the gate open as usual, passed through the paved grove up to
the palace door, and entered the vestibule. There in her cage lay the
spotted leopardess, apparently asleep or lifeless. The Little Ones
paused a moment to look at her. She leaped up rampant against the cage.
The horses reared and plunged; the elephants retreated a step. The
next instant she fell supine, writhed in quivering spasms, and lay
motionless. We rode into the great hall.

The princess yet leaned back in her chair in the shaft of sunlight, when
from the stones of the court came to her ears the noise of the horses’
hoofs. She started, listened, and shook: never had such sound been
heard in her palace! She pressed her hand to her side, and gasped. The
trampling came nearer and nearer; it entered the hall itself; moving
figures that were not shadows approached her through the darkness!

For us, we saw a splendour, a glorious woman centring the dark. Lona
sprang from her horse, and bounded to her. I sprang from mine, and
followed Lona.

“Mother! mother!” she cried, and her clear, lovely voice echoed in the
dome.

The princess shivered; her face grew almost black with hate, her
eyebrows met on her forehead. She rose to her feet, and stood.

“Mother! mother!” cried Lona again, as she leaped on the daïs, and flung
her arms around the princess.

An instant more and I should have reached them!--in that instant I saw
Lona lifted high, and dashed on the marble floor. Oh, the horrible sound
of her fall! At my feet she fell, and lay still. The princess sat down
with the smile of a demoness.

I dropped on my knees beside Lona, raised her from the stones, and
pressed her to my bosom. With indignant hate I glanced at the princess;
she answered me with her sweetest smile. I would have sprung upon her,
taken her by the throat, and strangled her, but love of the child was
stronger than hate of the mother, and I clasped closer my precious
burden. Her arms hung helpless; her blood trickled over my hands, and
fell on the floor with soft, slow little plashes.

The horses scented it--mine first, then the small ones. Mine reared,
shivering and wild-eyed, went about, and thundered blindly down the dark
hall, with the little horses after him. Lona’s stood gazing down at his
mistress, and trembling all over. The boys flung themselves from their
horses’ backs, and they, not seeing the black wall before them, dashed
themselves, with mine, to pieces against it. The elephants came on to
the foot of the daïs, and stopped, wildly trumpeting; the Little Ones
sprang upon it, and stood horrified; the princess lay back in her seat,
her face that of a corpse, her eyes alone alive, wickedly flaming. She
was again withered and wasted to what I found in the wood, and her side
was as if a great branding hand had been laid upon it. But Lona saw
nothing, and I saw but Lona.

“Mother! mother!” she sighed, and her breathing ceased.

I carried her into the court: the sun shone upon a white face, and the
pitiful shadow of a ghostly smile. Her head hung back. She was “dead as
earth.”

I forgot the Little Ones, forgot the murdering princess, forgot the
body in my arms, and wandered away, looking for my Lona. The doors and
windows were crowded with brute-faces jeering at me, but not daring to
speak, for they saw the white leopardess behind me, hanging her head
close at my heel. I spurned her with my foot. She held back a moment,
and followed me again.

I reached the square: the little army was gone! Its emptiness roused me.
Where were the Little Ones, HER Little Ones? I had lost her children!
I stared helpless about me, staggered to the pillar, and sank upon its
base.

But as I sat gazing on the still countenance, it seemed to smile a live
momentary smile. I never doubted it an illusion, yet believed what it
said: I should yet see her alive! It was not she, it was I who was lost,
and she would find me!

I rose to go after the Little Ones, and instinctively sought the gate
by which we had entered. I looked around me, but saw nothing of the
leopardess.

The street was rapidly filling with a fierce crowd. They saw me
encumbered with my dead, but for a time dared not assail me. Ere I
reached the gate, however, they had gathered courage. The women began
to hustle me; I held on heedless. A man pushed against my sacred burden:
with a kick I sent him away howling. But the crowd pressed upon me, and
fearing for the dead that was beyond hurt, I clasped my treasure closer,
and freed my right arm. That instant, however, a commotion arose in the
street behind me; the crowd broke; and through it came the Little Ones I
had left in the palace. Ten of them were upon four of the elephants; on
the two other elephants lay the princess, bound hand and foot, and quite
still, save that her eyes rolled in their ghastly sockets. The two other
Little Ones rode behind her on Lona’s horse. Every now and then the wise
creatures that bore her threw their trunks behind and felt her cords.

I walked on in front, and out of the city. What an end to the hopes with
which I entered the evil place! We had captured the bad princess, and
lost our all-beloved queen! My life was bare! my heart was empty!

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. "Disgusted," Lona spat, the word tasting like bile. "With these people, and specifically the women. I want to burn this place to the ground and ride out before the sun sets."

Her desire for flight cut through the air like a knife, sharp and desperate. I held her gaze, my expression hardening into something she would not recognize as maternal tenderness, but rather as the cold resolve of a commander facing a breached fortress.

"To retreat now is not escape, Lona. It is surrender. It is a voluntary failure where victory remains within our grasp," I said, my voice low and steady. "Far worse, it shatters the spirit of the Little Ones. Their morale collapses, and they become prey. If we withdraw, the Princess will hunt us down without hesitation. If we flee, the prophecy dies with us."

I stepped closer, forcing her to confront the gravity of the moment. "Mother and Daughter *must* meet. Perhaps your beauty will strike the Princess with such force that her heart turns against her own ambition. If she draws steel, I shall stand between you both. Should I find myself powerless to stop her, I will strike her hand with a blade, severing the threat to ensure your safety. I know the outcome is sealed; fate has decreed that our doom arrives today. But we fight until the last breath."

Without a flicker of doubt regarding the ancient bond binding me to the Princess—a truth I kept hidden from her—I laid out the strategy. Lona's eyes widened, the disgust fading into a dawning realization of duty. She nodded, agreeing instantly to follow me to the palace.

High atop one of the great towers, the Princess had watched the dawn break over the sleeping city. She had seen the dust clouds rising—the approach of the Little Ones' army. Terror, primal and overwhelming, seized her. Her attempt to annihilate them had failed; they were upon her. The prophecy was fulfilling itself in real-time.

When reason returned, she descended to the Black Hall, seeking the North Focus of the ellipse beneath the roof's opening. She needed to think. Thinking, for her, required a specific state of being: not the reality of her current form, but the idealized version she chose to inhabit. To facilitate this delusion, she had suspended a mirror above her, invisible in the gloom, angled to catch the direct rays of the meridian sun.

She waited. Shadows danced in the periphery, but she possessed an inner eye that allowed her to ignore them. Even the Shadow that accompanied her walks remained unseen to her, too absorbed in its own obscurity. Servants shivered, paralyzed by the beasts outside, refusing to leave the chamber where the Princess sat motionless, starving for the sun's return. Courage and will had drained from her; they could no longer sustain her.

At dawn, we selected twelve of the Little Ones—tall, brave boys—to escort us. We mounted our great horses, alongside the smaller mounts and the war-elephants. The Princess remained in the hall, waiting for the sun to grant her the illusion of her own divinity. The tide of light crept up the eastern horizon, but until the sun stood directly overhead, no ray could penetrate the black stone.

Then, it happened. The sun rose, ascending swiftly toward zenith. As we climbed the steep path to the palace, the celestial body climbed the dome of the great hall. It peered through the central aperture—and suddenly, the hall flooded with brilliance.

The Princess screamed. She sprang to her feet, a cry of absolute despair tearing from her throat. "Alas!" she wailed. "My whiteness!"

A massive black spot, covering half her side, was revealed against the marble floor. It was as dark as the stone itself. Clutching her robes, she collapsed back into her chair. The Shadow glided silently across the floor and vanished into the darkness.

We found the gate open as usual, passing through the paved grove to the palace door and entering the vestibule. There, in her cage, lay the spotted leopardess, seemingly lifeless. The Little Ones paused, mesmerized. Suddenly, the beast leaped, rampant against the bars. The horses reared and plunged; the elephants recoiled. In the next instant, the leopardess fell supine, writhing in quivering spasms before going utterly still.

We rode into the Great Hall. The Princess still leaned back in her chair, bathed in the shaft of sunlight, when the sound of hooves erupted from the courtyard. She started, listening, shaking. Never had such a cacophony been heard within her sanctuary. She pressed a hand to her side and gasped. The trampling drew nearer, invading the hall itself. Figures that were not shadows emerged from the darkness, approaching her.

For us, the scene transformed into a spectacle of splendor. A glorious woman centered the darkness, radiating power. Lona spurred her horse forward, bounding from the mount to reach her. I followed suit, springing from my steed.

"Mother! Mother!" Lona cried, her clear, lovely voice echoing off the domed ceiling.

The Princess shivered violently. Her face darkened with hate, her eyebrows knitting together until they touched. Rising to her feet, she stood rigid.

"Mother! Mother!" Lona shouted again, leaping onto the dais and throwing her arms around the Princess.

In that split second, I would have reached them—but I saw Lona lifted high, then dashed against the marble floor. The sound was horrific, a crack of bone meeting stone. She fell at my feet, lying still.

The Princess sat down, wearing the smile of a demoness. I dropped to my knees beside Lona, lifting her from the cold stones and pressing her to my bosom. Indignant hate burned in my eyes as I glanced at the Princess, but she answered with her sweetest, most venomous smile. Love for the child overwhelmed my hatred for the mother. I tightened my grip on my precious burden. Her arms hung limp; blood trickled over my hands, falling to the floor in soft, slow plashes.

The horses smelled it first—my mount, then the others. Mine reared, shivering and wild-eyed, thundering blindly down the dark hall, dragging the smaller horses in its wake. Lona's horse stood frozen, gazing down at his mistress, trembling uncontrollably. The boys threw themselves from their saddles, failing to see the black wall ahead, and crashed against it along with my own mount, reduced to fragments.

The elephants advanced to the foot of the dais, stopping abruptly, trumpeting wildly. The Little Ones sprang upon them, standing in horror. The Princess slumped back into her seat, her face that of a corpse, her eyes alone alive, wickedly flaming. She was withered and wasted, returning to the state I had found her in the woods, the black brand on her side unmistakable.

But Lona saw nothing. I saw only Lona.

"Mother... mother..." she sighed, her breathing ceasing.

I carried her into the courtyard. The sun illuminated a pale face, marked by the pitiful shadow of a ghostly smile. Her head hung back. She was dead as earth.

I forgot the Little Ones. I forgot the murdering Princess. I forgot the body in my arms. I wandered away, searching for my Lona. Doors and windows burst open, crowded with brute-faced figures jeering at me, yet none dared speak, for they saw the white leopardess trailing behind me, head bowed low at my heel. I spurned her with my foot. She hesitated, then followed again.

I reached the square. The little army was gone. Its absence roused a terrifying emptiness. Where were the Little Ones? *Her* Little Ones? I had lost her children! Staring helplessly about me, I staggered to a pillar and sank upon its base.

As I sat gazing at the still countenance of the leopardess, it seemed to offer a live, momentary smile. I never doubted it was an illusion, yet I believed its message: *I should yet see her alive!* No, it was not she who was lost; it was I. She would find me!

Rising to pursue the Little Ones, I instinctively sought the gate by which we had entered. Looking around, I saw nothing of the leopardess. The street was rapidly filling with a fierce crowd. They saw me encumbered with my dead, but for a time, they dared not assault me. Before I reached the gate, however, they gathered courage. Women began to hustle me; I held on heedless. A man pushed against my sacred burden; I kicked him away, sending him howling.

The crowd pressed in, and fearing further harm to the dead, I clasped my treasure tighter, freeing my right arm. Instantly, a commotion erupted behind me. The crowd broke apart, and through the gap came the Little Ones I had left in the palace.
